title: Facial Orthography Boundary
subtitle: Unicode Sutton SignWriting and renderer-supplied facial composition
summary: A practitioner-facing boundary note: the official Unicode Sutton SignWriting block is useful as a repertoire and Unicode-specific composition model, but its facial-diacritic model is not production-compatible with general Sutton facial writing because it cannot preserve authored facial arrangement.
synopsis: This note is a practitioner guide for choosing text models, tools, corpora, datasets, archives, publications, and educational workflows for Sutton SignWriting. It states that the official Unicode Sutton SignWriting block provides a character repertoire and Unicode-specific composition model, but it is not the Sutton production text model for complete written signs. The official facial-diacritic model represents faces as U+1D9FF SIGNWRITING HEAD plus facial marks. For general FSW/SWU facial expressions, that sequence cannot supply a lossless production migration path by itself because authored facial arrangement is not present in the representation. The note gives practical guidance: use official Unicode SignWriting for repertoire, citation, standards discussion, Unicode-model research, limited symbol display, and work scoped to the official block; use FSW/SWU, Sutton-compatible tooling, or an equivalent coordinate-preserving production model for complete written signs, dictionaries, corpora, education, archives, datasets, AI, and machine-learning workflows. It explains why the issue is structural, why it is not merely a font problem, why spatial authorship matters, and why the 2012 mapping claims do not establish an isomorphism between authored Sutton facial composition and HEAD plus facial marks.

bullets: Unicode block: repertoire and Unicode-specific composition
Do not treat official support as production interchange
slides.speech: This boundary note is for people choosing tools, corpora, datasets, archives, publications, and educational workflows. The official Unicode Sutton SignWriting block is useful as a character repertoire and Unicode-specific composition model. It is not the Sutton production text model for complete written signs. The practical rule is direct: use the official block for repertoire, citation, Unicode-model research, limited symbol display, and work scoped to that model. Use FSW/SWU, Sutton-compatible tooling, or an equivalent coordinate-preserving production model for production Sutton SignWriting.
slides.notes: Open as practitioner guidance, not a standards request.

slides.title: Facial Model Fails
slides.summary: HEAD plus facial marks cannot preserve authored facial arrangement by itself.

image_prompts.concrete: A comparison of authored SignWriting facial composition with a Unicode head-plus-mark sequence
image_prompts.abstract: Authored spatial arrangement contrasted with a component list

bullets: Simple faces can hide the issue
slides.speech: The decisive technical point is structural. The official facial-diacritic model represents facial writing as U+1D9FF SIGNWRITING HEAD plus nonspacing facial marks. For general FSW/SWU facial expressions, that sequence cannot supply a lossless production migration path by itself because authored facial arrangement is not present in the representation. A renderer must decide ordering, attachment, hierarchy, collision handling, normal arrangements, valid combinations, and what counts as the same face. Those are orthographic assumptions, not just drawing decisions.
slides.notes: Stress missing stored data, not general opposition to fonts or rendering.

slides.title: Not A Font Problem
slides.summary: The question is whether the stored text preserves the authored face before rendering.

image_prompts.concrete: A font renderer drawing a face from a component list beside stored SignWriting source with explicit authored placement
image_prompts.abstract: Rendering output separated from text identity

bullets: Stored text must identify the written face
Better fonts cannot recover missing authorship
Complex-script shaping analogy does not settle the issue
slides.speech: The objection is not that visible text needs rendering. The issue is where the authored written information is stored. In Sutton production SignWriting, the writer's facial composition is part of the text model. In the Unicode-specific facial model, the author supplies HEAD plus marks and the renderer constructs the face. A better font may draw a plausible face, but it cannot recover authored facial arrangement from data that never stored it.

slides.title: Spatial Authorship
slides.summary: Sutton SignWriting uses authored spatial relations as written information.

image_prompts.concrete: Sutton SignWriting symbols arranged on a two-dimensional writing space with coordinates and facial components

bullets: FSW/SWU preserve selected symbols and coordinates
slides.speech: Sutton SignWriting conveys meaning through authored spatial relations. Facial writing is not exempt from that principle. The question is not whether every facial placement difference is canonical spelling today. The question is whether a text model should discard authored facial arrangement before communities have had the chance to compare, teach, normalize, reject, revise, or standardize written forms. A coordinate-preserving production model keeps that capacity available.
slides.notes: Frame preservation as community capacity, not just current correctness.

slides.title: Mapping Boundary
slides.summary: Mapping symbol identifiers is not the same as preserving authored facial composition.

image_prompts.concrete: A mapping table showing Unicode symbol identifiers separated from an external coordinate-bearing production protocol
image_prompts.abstract: Identifier mapping separated from production interchange

bullets: N4342 mapping claims have a scope
Symbol mapping is not facial isomorphism
Two authored faces can collapse to one sequence
Extra coordinates can carry production data
Then compatibility comes from the extra protocol
slides.speech: The 2012 mapping claim does not settle this boundary. It may describe mappings among certain symbol identifiers, especially base, fill, and rotation structures. It does not establish an isomorphism between authored Sutton facial composition and HEAD plus facial marks. A higher-level protocol can use Unicode characters as symbol identifiers while separately carrying authored coordinates or facial arrangement data, but then production compatibility comes from that coordinate-bearing protocol, not from the official facial-diacritic sequence.
slides.notes: Close on the technical heart: identifiers are not the same as authored arrangement.
